title: Solids, liquids and gases: why water takes the shape of its glass

summary.text: Pour water from a tumbler into a tall, thin bottle, and it looks like more. Pour it into a wide bowl, and it looks like less. Your child tests this, then pours the water back to see. A solid, like a steel spoon or an ice cube, keeps its own shape wherever you put it. A liquid, like water or milk, flows and takes the shape of whatever holds it. A gas, like air or steam, spreads out to fill every corner. Ice, water and steam are the same water in three different states.
summary.art: A glass tumbler with a bindi stuck on the side as a line, a tall thin bottle and a wide glass bowl, each holding the same amount of water at different heights, with an ice cube on a steel plate beside them.

intro.hook: Fill a glass tumbler halfway with water. Now imagine pouring it into a tall, thin bottle. Will there be more water, less water, or the same?
intro.text: Many children say the thin bottle will have more, because the water will stand taller. Some say less. You are going to pour it and find out. Water can change its shape in a moment. An ice cube cannot. Why is that? This unit answers that question, and you will test the answer yourself.
intro.art: A child holding a half-full glass tumbler over a tall thin bottle, with a thinking bubble showing the bottle full to the top.

outcomes: By the end I can sort things into solids, liquids and gases, and say why.
By the end I can say that a solid keeps its own shape, a liquid flows and takes the shape of its container, and a gas spreads out to fill all the space it has.
By the end I can show that water poured into a new shape is still the same amount of water.
By the end I can say that ice, water and steam are the same water, as a solid, a liquid and a gas.
By the end I can explain that real steam is invisible, and the white cloud above a kettle is tiny drops of water.
By the end I can guess first, give a reason, and then say what my test showed.

terms.meaning: A solid keeps its own shape. It does not flow, and it does not need a container.
terms.example: A steel spoon, a stone, a wooden block and an ice cube are solids.
terms.art: A steel spoon, a small stone and an ice cube sitting on a plate, each keeping its own shape.

terms.meaning: A liquid flows. It has no shape of its own, so it takes the shape of whatever holds it.
terms.example: Water, milk, oil and rasam are liquids. Pour rasam from a pot into a bowl, and it takes the shape of the bowl.
terms.art: Milk being poured from a steel tumbler into a katori, flowing and filling the bowl.

terms.meaning: A gas spreads out to fill all the space it can get to. Most gases cannot be seen.
terms.example: Air is a gas. Blow up a balloon, and the air fills the whole balloon, not just the bottom.
terms.art: A round balloon being blown up, with faint arrows inside showing air spreading to every side.

terms.meaning: Whether something is a solid, a liquid or a gas. These are the three states we see most.
terms.example: Water can be in all three states: ice, liquid water and steam.
terms.art: Three panels: ice cubes, water in a tumbler, and the clear space just above a kettle spout.

terms.meaning: To move along and spread, the way water runs when you pour it.
terms.example: Water flows down a drain. Honey flows too, but slowly.
terms.art: Water flowing out of a tap into a steel bucket.

terms.meaning: Something that holds things inside it, such as a tumbler, a bottle, a box or a bag.
terms.example: A water bottle is a container for water.
terms.art: A row of containers: a steel tumbler, a plastic bottle, a box and a cloth bag.

terms.meaning: To change from a solid into a liquid, when it gets warm.
terms.example: An ice cube melts into water on a warm plate. Ghee melts in a hot pan.
terms.art: An ice cube on a steel plate with a small pool of water around it.

terms.meaning: To change from a liquid into a solid, when it gets very cold.
terms.example: Water freezes into ice in the freezer.
terms.art: An ice tray full of water going into a freezer, and the same tray full of ice coming out.

terms.meaning: Water as a gas. It comes from water that is boiling. Real steam is invisible.
terms.example: Just above a kettle spout there is a small clear gap. That is where the real steam is.
terms.art: A steel kettle on a stove, with a clear gap just above the spout and a white cloud higher up.

explanations.context: This card explains what makes something a solid.
explanations.definition: A solid is something that keeps its own shape. It stays the same shape when you move it into a new container.
explanations.description: Put a steel spoon in a tumbler, then in a bowl, then on a plate. It is the same spoon shape every time. An ice cube is a solid too. In our test, the ice cube was too big to go into the thin bottle, because it could not change its shape to fit. You can change a solid's shape by pushing, cutting or breaking it. But on its own, a solid stays the way it is.
examples: A stone keeps its shape in your hand or in a bucket.
An ice cube would not go into the thin bottle.
A wooden block stays a block wherever you put it.
explanations.art: One steel spoon shown three times: in a tumbler, in a bowl and on a plate, the same shape each time.

explanations.concept: Liquids flow and take the shape of their container
explanations.context: This card explains what happened in our test, when we poured one tumbler of water into a thin bottle and a wide bowl.
explanations.definition: A liquid flows. It has no shape of its own, so it takes the shape of whatever holds it. Its amount stays the same.
explanations.description: In the thin bottle, the water stood tall. In the wide bowl, it spread out low and flat. It looked like more, then less. But when we poured it back, it came up to the same bindi line on the tumbler. The shape changed. The amount did not. A liquid also always settles at the bottom of its container, with a flat top.
examples: Water from the thin bottle filled the tumbler back to the bindi line.
Rasam poured from a pot takes the shape of each bowl.
Coconut water takes the shape of the inside of the coconut.
explanations.art: The same water in a tall thin bottle, a wide bowl and a tumbler, with arrows showing it poured back to the same line.

explanations.concept: Gases spread out to fill every corner
explanations.context: This card explains what a gas does, using the three bags we squeezed.
explanations.definition: A gas spreads out to fill all the space it can get to. It has no shape of its own, and it does not settle at the bottom.
explanations.description: In the three bags, the water lay at the bottom of its bag. The air filled the whole bag, right up to the top corners. When you squeezed one end, the air pushed into the other end. Most gases cannot be seen, so we notice them by what they do. Cooking gas in a cylinder is squeezed so hard that most of it is a liquid. It turns into a gas as it comes out.
examples: Air fills a balloon to its round shape.
Air filled the tied bag up to every corner.
Bubbles in a glass of soda are a gas.
explanations.art: Three polythene bags side by side: one with a stone lying at the bottom, one with water at the bottom, and one puffed full of air.

explanations.concept: Ice, water and steam are the same water
explanations.context: This card explains how water can be a solid, a liquid and a gas.
explanations.definition: Ice is water as a solid. Liquid water is water as a liquid. Steam is water as a gas. Cooling and warming change water from one state to another.
explanations.description: Water freezes into ice when it gets very cold. Ice melts back into water when it gets warm. Water boils when it gets very hot, and turns into steam. Real steam is invisible. Look just above a kettle spout: the small clear gap is the steam. A little higher, the steam cools and turns back into tiny drops of liquid water. Those drops are the white cloud we see. It is the same water all the way through.
examples: Ice cubes melt into water in a glass of nannari sherbet.
Water in an idli pot boils, and steam cooks the idlis.
Snow on the Himalayas melts and flows down into the Ganga.
explanations.art: A circle of three pictures with arrows: an ice cube melting into water, water boiling into steam, and steam cooling into drops on a steel lid.

explanations.concept: Why are they so different? Tiny particles
explanations.context: This card gives a first look at why solids, liquids and gases behave so differently. You will learn more about it in Class 3.
explanations.definition: Everything is made of tiny particles, far too small to see. How tightly they hold on to each other decides whether something is a solid, a liquid or a gas.
explanations.description: In a solid, the particles hold on tight and stay in their places. That is why a solid keeps its shape. In a liquid, the particles stay close, but they slide past each other. That is why a liquid flows. In a gas, the particles fly apart and move around freely. That is why a gas spreads out. When ice melts, the water particles loosen their hold. When water boils, they fly apart.
examples: Ice: water particles holding on tight.
Water: the same particles sliding past each other.
Steam: the same particles flying apart.
explanations.art: Three boxes: dots packed in neat rows for a solid, dots close but jumbled for a liquid, and dots far apart with motion lines for a gas.

agreed.text: A solid keeps its own shape, a liquid takes the shape of its container, and a gas spreads out to fill its container.
agreed.evidence: In the three bags, the stone stayed a stone shape, the water lay at the bottom, and the air filled the whole bag.

agreed.text: Pouring a liquid into a new shape does not change how much of it there is.
agreed.evidence: In our test, the water from the thin bottle and the wide bowl filled the tumbler back to the same bindi line.

agreed.text: Ice, liquid water and steam are the same substance in three states.
agreed.evidence: An ice cube on a plate melts into water. Water boiled in a pan disappears as steam, and that steam turns back into drops of water on a cold lid.

challenging.claim: Water in a tall, thin glass is more than the same water in a wide bowl, because it stands higher.
challenging.who: A common guess by young children. Alina Szeminska and Jean Piaget studied it in Switzerland and wrote about it in 1941.
challenging.for: The water really does stand higher in the thin glass, and we often judge amounts by height.
challenging.against: The thin glass is narrow, so the same water must stand higher in it. Pour it back into the first tumbler, and it reaches the same line.
challenging.context: This card is about a guess many children make before the pouring test.

challenging.claim: The white cloud above a kettle or a cooker is steam.
challenging.for: The cloud comes from the boiling water, and everyone calls it steam.
challenging.against: Real steam is a gas, and it is invisible. Look closely, and there is a clear gap just above the spout. The white cloud is tiny drops of liquid water, made as the steam cools in the air.
challenging.context: This card is about what we really see when water boils.

challenging.claim: Ice is heavier than water, because it is hard.
challenging.for: Ice feels hard and solid, and many hard things, like stones, sink.
challenging.against: Ice floats in a tumbler of water. When water freezes, it spreads out and takes up a little more space, about one-tenth more. So a cube of ice is lighter than the same size of water.
challenging.context: This card is about whether ice is heavier or lighter than water.

big_questions.q: The water looked like more in the thin bottle. Why do our eyes get fooled?
big_questions.hint: What do your eyes look at first: how high the water is, or how wide the container is?

big_questions.q: When ice melts, where does its shape go?
big_questions.hint: Was the shape part of the water, or part of the ice tray it froze in?

big_questions.q: Is set curd a solid or a liquid?
big_questions.hint: You can cut it with a spoon. But stir it hard, and it flows.

big_questions.q: Your body is more than half water. Why are you not a puddle?
big_questions.hint: What holds the water in your body, the way a bottle holds water?

big_questions.q: The same water can be ice, water and steam. Is it still the same water?
big_questions.hint: What changes, and what stays the same?

how_we_found_out.story: In 1611, in Florence, Italy, some learned men had an argument with the scientist Galileo Galilei. They asked a simple question: why does ice float? The men followed the old teachings of Aristotle, a thinker from ancient Greece. They said ice is water that the cold has squeezed and made thicker and heavier. It floats only because it is flat and wide, they said, like a thin chip of wood. Galileo did not agree. He said ice floats whatever its shape. If you push a lump of ice to the bottom of a bowl and let go, it rises back up. So ice must be lighter than the same amount of water. In 1612, he wrote a book about things that float in water. Today we know Galileo was right. When water freezes, it spreads out and takes up about one-tenth more space. That is why a full bottle of water can split in the freezer. You can check Galileo's test with an ice cube and a tumbler.
how_we_found_out.who: Galileo Galilei, an Italian scientist, and the followers of Aristotle who argued with him
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That ice is water made thicker and heavier by cold, and floats only because of its flat shape. Galileo showed that ice floats in any shape, and rises when pushed down, so it is lighter than water.
how_we_found_out.art: A man in 1600s Italian clothes pushing a lump of ice to the bottom of a glass bowl of water, while two other men in long robes watch, one pointing at a flat chip of wood floating beside it.

story.title: Who Got More Neer Mor?
story.note: Neer mor is thin, salty buttermilk with curry leaves and ginger, drunk in Tamil Nadu in the hot months. Kavya, Arjun and Paati are made up.
text: It was May in Chennai, and the afternoon was very hot. Kavya was eight. Her cousin Arjun was six, and he had come to stay for the holidays.

Paati, their grandmother, was making neer mor in the kitchen. She stirred curd and water together in a big steel vessel. She added salt, a little ginger and a few curry leaves. It smelled cool and green.
"Bring me two cups," said Paati.
Kavya brought a tall, thin glass bottle. Arjun brought a wide steel davara, the low bowl that goes under a coffee tumbler.

Paati filled one small steel tumbler with neer mor, right to the brim. She poured it carefully through a small funnel into Kavya's thin bottle. Then she filled the same tumbler to the brim again, and poured it into Arjun's davara.
Arjun looked at the two cups. Then he looked again. His face went red.
"Kavya got more!" he said. "Look, hers goes up so high. Mine is only at the bottom."
It was true that Kavya's neer mor stood tall in the thin bottle. Arjun's lay low and flat in the wide davara.
"Paati poured the same tumbler both times," said Kavya. "I watched."
"But it looks like more," said Arjun.
Kavya thought for a moment. Then she took two small steel tumblers, exactly like the one Paati had used.

"Watch," she said. She poured her neer mor from the thin bottle into the first tumbler. It came right up to the brim. Then she poured Arjun's neer mor from the davara into the second tumbler. It came right up to the brim too.
Arjun bent down until his nose nearly touched the tumblers. The two tops were level.
"They are the same," he said slowly. "But in the bottle it was tall."

"The bottle is thin," said Kavya. "So the neer mor has to stand tall to fit inside. The davara is wide, so it spreads out low. Neer mor has no shape of its own. It takes the shape of whatever holds it. The amount stays the same."
Paati smiled and said nothing. She only handed each of them their own tumbler back.
Arjun drank half of his. Then he had an idea. "I want ice in mine," he said.
Paati took the ice tray out of the freezer and twisted it. Out popped a row of square ice cubes.

Arjun had poured his neer mor back into the thin bottle, because he liked how tall it looked. He tried to push an ice cube into the mouth of the bottle. It would not go in. He turned it this way and that way. It was too big.
"The neer mor went in easily," he said. "Why won't the ice?"
"The neer mor can change its shape to fit," said Kavya. "The ice cube is a solid. It keeps its own shape. It is still a square, and the square is too big."
"Put it in the davara," said Paati. "Wait a little."
Arjun put the ice cube in the empty davara. He sat on the kitchen step and watched it. The corners went round first. A little pool of water grew around it. The cube got smaller and smaller.
After about twenty minutes, there was no cube at all. There was only cold water in the bottom of the davara, lying flat and low.
Arjun picked up the davara and poured the water into his thin bottle. It went in easily, every drop.
"The same ice went in!" he said. "Once it was water."
"When ice melts, it becomes a liquid," said Kavya. "Then it can take any shape."
Just then, the idli pot on the stove began to hiss. Paati lifted the lid, and a white cloud rose up.
"Is that the water too?" asked Arjun.

"Yes," said Paati. "The water in the pot boiled and turned into steam. Look just above the pot, where the cloud begins. Do you see a clear gap? That is the real steam. It is a gas, so you cannot see it. Higher up, it cools and turns back into tiny drops of water. The drops make the white cloud."
Arjun looked at the ice tray, the cold water in his bottle and the white cloud over the stove.
"Ice, water and steam," he said. "All the same water."
"All the same water," said Paati, and she gave him the first hot idli.
story.epiphany: Neer mor and water have no shape of their own. They take the shape of whatever holds them, and the amount stays the same. Ice keeps its own shape until it melts. Ice, water and steam are the same water.
ask: Why did Arjun think Kavya had more neer mor?
How did Kavya show that they both had the same amount?
Why would the ice cube not go into the bottle, when the water from it did?
art: A hot Chennai kitchen with a grandmother pouring buttermilk, a girl holding a tall thin bottle, and a small boy frowning at a wide steel davara.
A small boy sitting on a kitchen step watching an ice cube melt in a steel davara, while steam rises from an idli pot on the stove behind him.

experiments.title: One Tumbler, Three Shapes: does the amount of water change?
experiments.context: In this experiment you pour one tumbler of water into a tall, thin bottle and into a wide bowl. Then you pour it back to see if the amount changed. Last, you try the same with an ice cube.
experiments.question: When we pour water into a container of a different shape, is there more water, less water, or the same amount?
experiments.predict: Look at the thin bottle and the wide bowl. When the water goes into the thin bottle, will there be more, less or the same? What about the wide bowl? And when we pour it back, will it reach the bindi line? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We use the same water every time, and fill the same tumbler to the same bindi line. We pour slowly over a tray, so no water is lost. We always look at the tumbler at eye level.
results_table: My guess: more, less or the same?
How did it look in the container?
Poured back: at the bindi, above it, or below it?

materials.item: a glass tumbler, or a clear plastic cup
a bindi sticker or a small strip of sticky tape, to mark a line
a tall, thin clear bottle, such as an empty 200 or 250 ml drink bottle, washed out
a wide clear bowl or a wide plastic food box (a wide steel bowl works too, but you cannot see through it)
a small kitchen funnel, or a cone rolled from a sheet of paper
water, with a few drops of turmeric water or food colour so it is easy to see (optional)
two or three ice cubes from the freezer, and a steel spoon
a tray or a big steel plate to work on, and a cloth for drips

schedule.what: Mark the tumbler. Guess. Pour the water into the thin bottle and back, then into the wide bowl and back. Try an ice cube in each. Say what you found.

experiments.record: Write your guesses at the top. Fill in the table. Draw the water in the tumbler, the thin bottle and the wide bowl, at the heights you saw.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
rows: Tall, up to the shoulder of the bottle
Low and flat, only a finger deep
At the bindi, maybe a hair below
Too big for the bottle mouth

setup.art: A glass tumbler on a tray, half full of yellow water, with a red bindi stuck on the outside exactly at the top of the water.
setup.caption: 1. Fill the tumbler halfway. Stick a bindi at the top of the water.

setup.art: A child pouring the water from the tumbler through a small funnel into a tall thin clear bottle, over a tray.
setup.caption: 2. Pour the water into the thin bottle. How tall does it stand?

setup.art: The same water poured from the thin bottle back into the tumbler, with the top of the water level with the bindi.
setup.caption: 3. Pour it back. Does it reach the bindi?

setup.art: The water lying low and flat in a wide clear bowl, then poured back into the tumbler up to the bindi.
setup.caption: 4. Do the same with the wide bowl.

setup.art: A child trying to push an ice cube into the narrow mouth of the thin bottle, and the cube not fitting.
setup.caption: 5. Try an ice cube in each container.

flow.do: 1. Put the tray on a table. 2. Fill the tumbler about halfway with water. 3. Your child sticks the bindi on the outside, exactly at the top of the water. 4. Show them the thin bottle and the wide bowl.
flow.say: This bindi marks how much water we have. Now look at the thin bottle and the wide bowl. If I pour this water into the thin bottle, will there be more, less or the same? What about the bowl? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Stick the bindi at the top of the water. Look at the bottle and the bowl. Guess: more, less or the same? Say why.

ask.q: Will there be more water in the thin bottle? Why?
good: More, because it will go up high.
The same, because it is the same water.
Less, because the bottle is small.

flow.parent: Don't say if a guess is right. Many children of this age say the thin bottle will have more, because the water will stand taller. Any guess with a reason is good. Write the guesses down.
flow.context: This is the first step of the pouring test. You mark the water and guess.

flow.do: 1. Put the funnel in the mouth of the thin bottle. 2. Your child pours all the water from the tumbler into it, slowly. 3. Hold the bottle next to the empty tumbler. 4. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: Pour slowly, so we don't lose any. Now look. How high is the water in the bottle? Does it look like more, or less, than before?
flow.kid: Pour the water into the bottle, slowly. Look at it. Does it look like more?

ask.q: How does the water look in the thin bottle?
good: It goes up much higher.
It looks like more water.

flow.parent: In a thin bottle the water stands much higher than it did in the tumbler. Let your child say what they see. Don't explain yet.
flow.context: In this step of the pouring test, you pour the water into the thin bottle.

flow.do: 1. Your child pours the water from the bottle back into the tumbler. 2. They put their eye level with the bindi. 3. Write the result in the table.
flow.say: Now pour it back into the tumbler. Bend down so your eye is level with the bindi. Is the water above the bindi, below it, or right at it?
flow.kid: Pour it back into the tumbler. Bend down. Look at the bindi. Is the water at the bindi?

ask.q: Where is the water now?
good: Right at the bindi.
A tiny bit below, because some drops stayed in the bottle.

flow.parent: The water comes back to the bindi, or a hair below it, because a few drops cling to the inside of the bottle. Point that out if the water is slightly low.

check.q: The water went into the thin bottle and came back to the bindi. What does that show?
options: It was the same amount of water all along
check.why: The water only looked like more because the bottle is thin, so it had to stand tall. The amount never changed.

flow.context: In this step of the pouring test, you pour the water back to see if the amount changed.

flow.do: 1. Your child pours the water from the tumbler into the wide bowl. 2. Ask how it looks. 3. Then they pour it back into the tumbler, over the tray. 4. Check the bindi again and write it down.
flow.say: Now the wide bowl. Pour it in. Does it look like more or less? Now pour it back. Where is the water now?
flow.kid: Pour the water into the bowl. More or less? Now pour it back. Is it at the bindi?

ask.q: What happened this time?
good: In the bowl it looked like only a little.
Back in the tumbler, it came to the bindi again.

flow.parent: Pouring from a wide bowl can spill. Tip it slowly over the tray, or use the funnel. If a little spills, count it as a drip, not as water that vanished.
flow.context: In this step of the pouring test, you pour the water into the wide bowl and back.

flow.do: 1. Give your child an ice cube and a steel spoon. 2. They put each one in the tumbler, then the bowl, then try the bottle mouth. 3. Ask the questions below. 4. Listen to their answer before you explain.
flow.say: The water changed its shape for every container. Now try an ice cube and a spoon. Do they change shape? Why could the water get into the bottle when the ice cube cannot?
flow.kid: Put the ice cube in each one. Try the spoon too. Do they change shape? Why can water get in, but not the ice?

ask.q: Why did the water fit in the thin bottle but the ice cube did not?
good: Water changes its shape to fit.
The ice cube keeps its own shape, and it is too big.

flow.parent: After your child answers, say it plainly. Water is a liquid. It has no shape of its own, so it takes the shape of whatever holds it, and the amount stays the same. The ice cube and the spoon are solids. They keep their own shape. If your ice cube is small enough to slip into the bottle, look closely: it is still a cube inside.
flow.think: If the ice cube melts, will its water fit in the bottle?
flow.context: This is the last step of the pouring test. You compare the water with an ice cube and a spoon.

experiments.title: The Ice Glove: what shape will frozen water be?
experiments.context: In this experiment you freeze water inside a clean plastic glove or a balloon. The next day you peel it off, and watch the shape of the ice as it melts on a plate.
experiments.question: If we freeze water in a glove, what shape will the ice be? And what happens to that shape as the ice melts?
experiments.predict: What shape will the ice be when we peel off the glove? When it melts on the plate, what shape will the water be? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We use one glove and one ordinary ice cube from a tray, side by side on the same plate in the same room. We look at both every 10 minutes, so we compare them the same way.
results_table: What the ice hand looks like
What the ice cube looks like
What the water on the plate looks like

materials.item: a clean, new plastic or rubber kitchen glove with no holes (or a small balloon)
a rubber band or a piece of string to close it
water
space in the freezer, and a steel plate to lay it on
a big steel plate with a rim, or a tray, for melting
one ordinary ice cube
a clock or a phone timer

experiments.safety: A grown-up cuts the glove off the ice with scissors. Hold frozen ice with a cloth, because very cold ice can stick to wet fingers.

schedule.what: Fill the glove with water, close it, and lay it flat in the freezer overnight.
Peel or cut off the glove. Put the ice hand and an ice cube on a plate. Look every 10 minutes and fill in the table.

experiments.record: Draw the ice hand when you first take it out, after 10 minutes and after 20 minutes. Draw the water on the plate at the end.

setup.art: A child holding a plastic glove under a tap while a grown-up holds the wrist open, the fingers swelling with water.
setup.caption: 1. Fill the glove with water. Close it with a rubber band.

setup.art: The water-filled glove lying flat on a steel plate inside a freezer.
setup.caption: 2. Lay it flat in the freezer overnight.

setup.art: A grown-up cutting a plastic glove away from a solid ice hand on a steel plate, with fingers clearly shaped.
setup.caption: 3. Next day, a grown-up cuts the glove off.

setup.art: An ice hand with rounded, shrinking fingers on a steel plate, an ice cube beside it, and a flat pool of water spreading over the plate.
setup.caption: 4. Watch the ice hand and the ice cube melt.

flow.do: 1. Hold the glove open under the tap. 2. Your child fills it with water until the fingers are fat. 3. Squeeze out any big air bubble. 4. Close it tightly with the rubber band. 5. Lay it flat on a plate in the freezer.
flow.say: The water is a liquid, so it fills the shape of the glove. What shape will it be after a night in the freezer? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Fill the glove with water. Close it tight. Put it in the freezer. Guess what shape it will be.

ask.q: What shape will the ice be?
good: A hand, because the water filled the glove.
A lump, because ice is a cube.

flow.parent: Lay it flat with the fingers spread, so they freeze apart. A home freezer freezes it overnight. A small single-door fridge freezer may need a whole day.
flow.wait: Leave it in the freezer overnight.

flow.do: 1. Take the glove out of the freezer. 2. Cut the glove open with scissors and peel it off. 3. Put the ice hand on the big plate. 4. Put an ordinary ice cube next to it.
flow.say: Look. What shape is the ice? The glove is gone. So what is holding the ice in the shape of a hand?
flow.kid: Look at the ice. What shape is it? The glove is gone. Is it still a hand?

ask.q: Why is it still a hand when the glove is gone?
good: Ice is a solid, so it keeps its shape.
It froze in the glove shape and stays that way.

flow.parent: The ice keeps the shape of the glove, with every finger. A solid keeps its own shape, even after the container is gone.

flow.do: 1. Start the timer. 2. Every 10 minutes, your child looks at the ice hand, the ice cube and the water on the plate. 3. They draw or say what has changed.
flow.say: What is happening to the fingers? Where is the water going? What shape is the water on the plate?
flow.kid: Look every 10 minutes. What is happening to the fingers? What shape is the water?

ask.q: What shape is the water on the plate?
good: Flat, spread over the plate.
It took the shape of the plate.

flow.parent: The fingertips round off first. Water spreads flat across the plate, up to the rim. In a warm room the thin fingers may melt off in 20 to 40 minutes. The thick palm takes much longer.

flow.do: 1. Ask the questions below. 2. Listen before you explain.
flow.say: While it was ice, it kept the shape of a hand. As it melts, what shape is the water? Where did the hand shape go?
flow.kid: As ice, it was a hand. As water, it spreads flat. Where did the hand shape go?

ask.q: Where did the hand shape go?
good: It went away, because water takes the shape of the plate.
The water has no shape of its own.

flow.parent: The hand shape came from the glove. As ice, the water kept it. As soon as it melts, the water has no shape of its own, so it takes the shape of the plate.

check.q: Why does the melted water spread flat over the plate?
options: Because a liquid takes the shape of whatever holds it
Because the ice was a hand
check.why: A liquid has no shape of its own. Here the plate holds the water, so the water takes the plate's flat shape.

activities.title: Three Bags: a solid, a liquid and a gas
activities.context: In this activity you fill three clear polythene bags: one with a stone, one with water and one with air. You turn them, squeeze them and watch what each one does.

materials.item: three clear polythene bags with no holes, such as zip bags or food bags
a small stone, a wooden block or a steel spoon
about one tumbler of water
three rubber bands, or tie a knot in each bag
a tray or a bucket to work over

schedule.what: Fill three bags: a stone, water and air. Turn them upside down, squeeze them, and say what each one does.

activities.record: Draw the three bags, held upside down. Show where the stone, the water and the air are in each bag.

setup.art: Three clear polythene bags on a tray: one with a small stone, one with water, and one blown up with air and tied.
setup.caption: 1. Fill three bags: a stone, water and air. Close each one tight.

setup.art: A child holding all three bags upside down: the stone at the new bottom, the water at the new bottom, and the air bag still puffed full.
setup.caption: 2. Turn each bag upside down. Where does everything go?

setup.art: A child gently squeezing one end of the air bag, with the other end puffing out bigger.
setup.caption: 3. Squeeze one end of each bag gently.

flow.do: 1. Put the stone in the first bag and close it. 2. Pour the water into the second bag over the tray, and close it tightly. 3. Your child blows air into the third bag and you tie it quickly.
flow.say: One bag has a stone, one has water, and one has air. Now guess. When we turn them upside down, what will each one do? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Put a stone in one bag. Water in one bag. Blow air into one bag. Guess what each will do.
flow.parent: Use thick bags if you have them. Hold the water bag closed at the top and tie it well. Do it over a tray in case it leaks.

flow.do: 1. Your child turns each bag upside down, slowly. 2. Then they squeeze one end of each bag gently. 3. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: Turn each bag upside down. Where did the stone go? The water? The air? Now squeeze one end gently. What happens?
flow.kid: Turn each bag over. Where did each one go? Squeeze one end gently. What happens?

ask.q: What did each one do?
good: The stone stayed a stone and fell to the bottom.
The water ran to the new bottom of the bag.
The air stayed everywhere in the bag.

flow.parent: The stone keeps its shape and drops to the lowest point. The water flows to the lowest part and takes the shape of that end of the bag, with a flat top. The air fills the whole bag all the time. Squeeze one end, and the air pushes into the other end.

flow.do: 1. Lay the three bags side by side. 2. Ask the question below. 3. Then say the three words: solid, liquid, gas.
flow.say: The stone kept its own shape. The water took the shape of the bottom of its bag. The air filled the whole bag. Which one is the solid? The liquid? The gas?
flow.kid: Which bag has a solid? Which has a liquid? Which has a gas?

ask.q: Which one filled the whole bag?
good: The air.
The gas, because a gas spreads out everywhere.

flow.parent: A solid keeps its own shape. A liquid takes the shape of the bottom of its container. A gas spreads out to fill all of it.

check.q: Which bag stayed puffed full, even upside down?
check.why: Air is a gas. A gas spreads out to fill all the space in its container, so it filled the whole bag every way up.

activities.title: Where Is the Steam? Look closely at a boiling kettle
activities.context: In this activity a grown-up boils water in a kettle or a pan with a spout. You stand back and look for a clear gap just above the spout.

materials.item: a steel kettle, or a covered pan or pressure cooker that lets out steam (a grown-up uses it)
water
a dark cloth, a dark plate or a dark wall behind the kettle, so the cloud is easy to see

activities.safety: Steam burns badly, even though you cannot see it. A grown-up works the stove. The child stands at least one big step away and never puts a hand, a spoon or a face near the spout.

schedule.what: A grown-up boils water. Stand back and look for the clear gap just above the spout. Then look at the white cloud above it.

activities.record: Draw the kettle. Colour the white cloud. Leave the clear gap just above the spout empty, and label it 'steam'.

setup.art: A grown-up putting a steel kettle of water on a gas stove, with a dark cloth hung on the wall behind it, and a child standing one big step back.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up boils water. Stand one big step back.

setup.art: Close-up of a kettle spout with a clear gap just above it, then a white cloud starting a little higher up.
setup.caption: 2. Look just above the spout. Can you see a clear gap?

flow.do: 1. Boil water in the kettle. 2. Hang or hold something dark behind it. 3. Your child stands at least one big step away. 4. Ask them to guess what they will see.
flow.say: When the water boils, it turns into steam. What colour do you think steam is? Why?
flow.kid: Stand one big step back. The water will boil. What colour is steam? Guess and say why.
flow.parent: Most children say steam is white. Let them guess. Keep them well back from the spout at all times.

flow.do: 1. When the kettle is steaming, point to the spout. 2. Ask your child to look at the tiny space just above it, before the white cloud starts.
flow.say: Look just above the spout, before the white cloud begins. What do you see there?
flow.kid: Look just above the spout. Is there a clear gap before the cloud?

ask.q: What is in the gap?
good: Nothing I can see.
It is clear, like air.

flow.parent: There is a small clear gap, usually about one or two finger-widths, between the spout and the white cloud. Real steam is in that gap. It is a gas, and it is invisible.

flow.do: 1. Turn off the stove. 2. Ask the question below. 3. Listen, then explain.
flow.say: The gap was clear, but the cloud is white. What do you think the white cloud is?
flow.kid: The gap is clear. The cloud is white. What is the white cloud?

ask.q: What is the white cloud?
good: Water drops.
Steam that cooled down and turned back into water.

flow.parent: Real steam is water as a gas, and you cannot see it. As it rises, it cools in the room air and turns back into tiny drops of liquid water. Those drops make the white cloud. Higher up, the cloud fades as the drops spread into the air.

options: In the clear gap just above the spout
check.why: Real steam is a gas, and it is invisible. The white cloud above it is tiny drops of liquid water.

activities.title: The Home Hunt: solids, liquids and gases
activities.context: In this activity you walk around your home and find solids, liquids and gases. You draw each one in the right column.

materials.item: a sheet of paper with three columns: solid, liquid, gas
a pencil

schedule.what: Walk around the home. Find 4 solids, 4 liquids and 2 gases. Draw each one in its column.

activities.record: The sheet with three columns, with at least 4 solids, 4 liquids and 2 gases drawn or written.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with three columns labelled solid, liquid and gas, and a pencil.
setup.caption: 1. Draw three columns: solid, liquid, gas.

setup.art: A child in a kitchen pointing at a bottle of coconut oil, a steel plate and a bubbling glass of soda.
setup.caption: 2. Walk around. Put each thing in a column.

flow.do: 1. Walk through the kitchen, bathroom and one more room together. 2. Your child finds 4 solids, 4 liquids and 2 gases. 3. They draw or write each one in its column.
flow.say: Find something that keeps its own shape. That is a solid. Find something that flows. That is a liquid. Now the hard one: can you find a gas?
flow.kid: Find 4 solids and 4 liquids. Then find 2 gases. Draw each one.
flow.parent: Gases are hard to find, because most are invisible. Hints: the air in a ball or a tyre, the bubbles in soda, the steam from cooking, the air you breathe out. Never open the cooking gas to look.

ask.q: What gas did you find?
good: The air in my football.
The bubbles in soda.
My breath.

flow.do: 1. Look at the sheet together. 2. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: Which column was easiest to fill? Which was hardest? Why were gases so hard to find?
flow.kid: Which column was easy? Which was hard? Why were gases hard?

ask.q: Why were gases hard to find?
good: You can't see most of them.
They spread out, so they are everywhere.

flow.parent: Most gases are invisible, so we find them by what they do: air puffs up a ball, and soda bubbles rise.

games.title: Solid, Liquid or Gas? A sorting card game
games.context: This is a sorting game. Each card names a thing. You put it under solid, liquid or gas, and say why.

printables.title: The three-column board, drawn on a big sheet of paper
items: Liquid: flows, takes the shape of its container
Gas: spreads out to fill all the space

items.b: Solid. It keeps its own shape.
Solid. Ice is water as a solid.
Solid. It keeps its own shape.
Solid. It keeps its own shape.
Solid. It keeps its own shape.
Solid, while it is frozen. When it melts, it becomes a liquid.
Liquid. It flows and takes the shape of the glass.
Liquid. It takes the shape of each bowl.
Liquid. It takes the shape of the inside of the coconut.
Liquid. It flows slowly, but it still takes the shape of its jar.
Liquid. When it cools, it can set into a soft solid.
Liquid. Rain is drops of liquid water.
Gas. It fills the whole balloon.

items.f: The bubbles in a glass of soda
items.b: Gas. The bubbles are a gas called carbon dioxide.

items.f: The clear gap above a kettle spout
items.b: Gas. That is real steam, which is invisible.
Gas. You breathe out air.

rules: Draw the board: a big sheet split into three columns, with the labels written at the top.
Shuffle the 16 cards and put them face down in a pile.
Take turns. Turn over the top card, read it, and put it in a column. Say why.
Then turn the card over and read the back. If you were right, keep the card in the column and score one point. If not, move it, and say why it goes there.
When all 16 are placed, the player with the most points wins. Playing alone, try to beat your own score next time.

setup.art: A big sheet of paper split into three columns labelled solid, liquid and gas, with a pile of small cards beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the board. Shuffle the cards.

setup.art: A child placing a card that says 'Coconut water' in the liquid column.
setup.caption: 2. Turn over a card. Put it in a column. Say why.

flow.do: 1. Draw the board with your child. 2. Cut out the cards. 3. Read the three labels together.
flow.say: Every card goes in one column. Ask yourself: does it keep its shape, does it flow, or does it spread out everywhere?
flow.kid: Draw the three columns. Read the labels. Cut out the cards.

flow.do: 1. Take turns turning over a card. 2. The player puts it in a column and says why. 3. Read the back and score.
flow.say: Honey. It flows very slowly. Is it a solid or a liquid? Why?
flow.kid: Turn over a card. Does it keep its shape? Does it flow? Does it spread out? Pick a column.

ask.q: Why did you put honey with the liquids?
good: It flows, even if slowly.
It takes the shape of the jar.

flow.parent: Honey and the kettle gap surprise most children. Honey is a liquid, because it flows and takes the shape of its jar. The clear gap above a kettle is real steam.

flow.do: 1. Look at the gas column. 2. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Look at the gas column. Could you see any of these, apart from the soda bubbles?
flow.kid: Look at the gas cards. Can you see any of them?

ask.q: Why are gases hard to see?
good: Most gases are invisible.
We see bubbles because they are inside a liquid.

games.title: Freeze, Flow, Fly! Be ice, water and steam
games.players: 2 or more players, with one caller
games.context: This is a moving game. The caller shows a card: ice, water or steam. The players move like a solid, a liquid or a gas.

items.b: Freeze close together and hold hands or shoulders. Do not move from your spot.
Stay close and touch shoulders, but slide past each other slowly.
Let go and spread out to every corner of the room.
Water turns to ice. Freeze close together.
Water turns to steam. Spread out to the corners.
Ice melts into water. Loosen up and slide.
Steam turns back into water drops. Come close and slide.

items.f: Pour the water into a bowl!
items.b: Water takes the shape of the bowl. Move to fill a circle on the floor.

items.f: Pour the water into a thin bottle!
items.b: Water takes the shape of the bottle. Line up close in a thin line.
Ice keeps its shape. Hold on tight. You cannot squeeze into a line.
A gas fills all the space. Spread out across the whole room.
Liquid milk freezes into a solid. Freeze close together.

rules: Clear a space in the middle of a room.
One person is the caller. Everyone else starts standing close together as 'water'.
The caller reads a card out loud. The players move the way the card says.
The caller reads the back, so everyone can check. Anyone who moved the wrong way sits out one turn.
After 12 cards, a new player becomes the caller.

setup.art: Two children and a grown-up standing close together in the middle of a room, holding a card that says 'Ice!'.
setup.caption: 1. Start close together. The caller reads a card.

setup.art: The same players spread out into the corners of the room, after the card 'Steam!'.
setup.caption: 2. Move like ice, water or steam.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards. 2. Clear a space. 3. Show the three moves: ice, water and steam.
flow.say: Ice holds tight and stays put. Water stays close but slides. Steam lets go and spreads out everywhere.
flow.kid: Ice: hold tight. Water: slide close. Steam: spread out.

flow.do: 1. Read each card. 2. Wait for the players to move. 3. Read the back to check.
flow.say: Ice in a thin bottle! What do you do?
flow.kid: Listen to the card. Move like ice, water or steam.
flow.parent: With only one child and one grown-up, the grown-up plays too and the child is the caller for half the cards.

flow.do: 1. At the end, ask the question below.
flow.say: When you were ice, could you fit into a thin line? When you were water, could you?
flow.kid: As ice, could you squeeze into a line? As water?

ask.q: Why could water fit into the thin bottle line, but ice could not?
good: Water slides and changes shape.
Ice holds tight and keeps its shape.

challenges.title: Move the Water Without a Cup
challenges.context: This is a problem-solving challenge. You must move 5 spoons of water from one katori to another, across the room, without using a cup, a bowl, a bottle or a spoon to carry it.
challenges.problem: Put 5 spoons of water in a katori in the kitchen. Get as much of it as you can into an empty katori on the other side of the room. You cannot carry it in a cup, a bowl, a bottle or a spoon.
constraints: No cups, bowls, bottles, spoons or other containers to carry the water.
You may take one hour if you need to.
materials: two katoris and a spoon to measure the water
a sponge, a cotton cloth, a towel, a polythene sheet, an ice tray and a freezer (choose what you like)
general: Soak the water up in a sponge or a cloth, carry it, and squeeze it out.
Try two different cloths, wet each with the same amount of water, and see which one carries more.
creative: Freeze the water in an ice tray, carry the ice cubes in your hand, and let them melt in the far katori. A solid can be carried without a container.
Roll a polythene sheet into a long slope, so the water flows down it into the far katori.
challenges.your_turn: Think of your own way. Test it. Then count how many spoons of water reached the far katori. Can you make your way better?

setup.art: A katori with water on a kitchen counter, an empty katori on a table across the room, and a sponge, a cloth, a polythene sheet and an ice tray laid out.
setup.caption: 1. Put 5 spoons of water in the first katori.

setup.art: A child carrying a dripping sponge across a room towards the empty katori.
setup.caption: 2. Move the water your own way, without a cup.

setup.art: A child spooning the collected water out of the far katori, counting.
setup.caption: 3. Count how many spoons reached the far katori.

flow.do: 1. Measure 5 spoons of water into the first katori. 2. Read the rules together. 3. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: Water has no shape of its own, so it needs something to hold it. What can hold water, without being a cup?
flow.kid: Water needs something to hold it. What could hold it, if not a cup?

ask.q: What could you use?
good: A sponge, because it soaks water up.
Freeze it, so it keeps its shape.

flow.do: 1. Your child chooses a way and tries it. 2. Let them try a second way if the first one spills a lot.
flow.say: Try your idea. Watch where the water goes.
flow.kid: Try your idea. Watch the water.

flow.do: 1. Spoon the water out of the far katori and count the spoons. 2. Ask the question below.
flow.say: How many spoons got there? Which way lost the least water? Why?
flow.kid: Count the spoons. Which way lost the least? Why?

ask.q: Why did freezing work?
good: Ice is a solid. It keeps its shape, so I could carry it.
It did not need a cup.

flow.parent: Freezing changes the water into a solid, which keeps its own shape and can be held in a hand. If your child did not think of it, ask: what if the water were not a liquid?

items.p: Draw a line from each word to what it does.
pairs: flows and takes the shape of its container
spreads out to fill all the space
items.why: These are the main words in this unit. Each state does something different with its shape.

items.p: In the pouring test, the water went into the thin bottle and then back into the tumbler. Where did it come to?
opts: Right at the bindi, or a hair below
items.why: It was the same water all along, so it came back to the same line. A few drops may stay in the bottle. Picking 'far above' may mean thinking the bottle made more water.
items.context: This question is about the pouring test. You pour one tumbler of water into a tall, thin bottle and into a wide bowl, then pour it back to a bindi line on the tumbler.

items.p: Sort these into solid, liquid and gas.
items.why: The spoon and ice keep their own shape. Milk and rasam flow and take the shape of their bowl. Air and soda bubbles are gases.

items.p: Draw the same water in the tumbler, in the thin bottle and in the wide bowl. Show how high it stood in each one.
items.a: The water at the bindi in the tumbler, tall in the thin bottle, and low and flat in the wide bowl.
items.why: A strong drawing shows three different heights, and a label such as 'same water' on all three.
items.context: This question is about the pouring test. You pour one tumbler of water into a tall, thin bottle and into a wide bowl, then pour it back to a bindi line on the tumbler.
items.art: Outlines of a tumbler, a tall thin bottle and a wide bowl side by side, all empty.

items.p: Water poured into a tall, thin bottle becomes more water, because it stands higher.
items.why: False. The bottle is thin, so the same water has to stand taller. Poured back, it reaches the same line.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: why would the ice cube not go into the thin bottle, when the water did?
items.a: The ice cube is a solid and keeps its own shape, so it was too big. Water is a liquid. It changes its shape to fit.
items.why: A strong answer says the ice keeps its shape and the water changes its shape.
items.context: This question is about the pouring test. You pour one tumbler of water into a tall, thin bottle and into a wide bowl, then pour it back to a bindi line on the tumbler.

items.p: Asha fills a tumbler to the bindi line 3 times and pours all of it into a big bucket. Then she pours the bucket back into the tumbler. How many times can she fill the tumbler to the line?
items.why: Pouring water into a new container does not change how much there is. 3 tumblers went in, so 3 tumblers come out.

items.p: Label each picture: solid, liquid or gas.
labels: the clear gap just above a kettle spout
items.why: These are the same water in three states. The clear gap is real steam, a gas you cannot see.
items.art: Three small pictures, each with an empty label line under it.

items.p: Meena and Divya are taking water on a long, hot train ride from Chennai to Madurai.

views.says: Freeze a bottle of water the night before. It stays cold for longer, and we drink it as it melts.
Take liquid water. We can drink it straight away, the moment we get thirsty.

items.ask: Whose plan would you choose? Give one reason. Then say one thing the other girl has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks one with a reason, such as 'ice stays cold for longer'. It also says what the other plan gets right, such as 'you can drink liquid water at once'.
items.why: Both plans have a good point. Frozen water stays cold for longer but must melt before you drink it. Liquid water is ready at once but warms up. Leave space at the top if you freeze a bottle, because water takes up a little more space as ice.

items.p: Three of these keep their own shape. Which one does not?
items.why: Buttermilk is a liquid. It takes the shape of whatever holds it. The other three are solids.

items.p: Gauri, a girl in Patna, blows up a balloon. Where does the air go?
opts: Only to the bottom of the balloon
items.why: Air is a gas, and a gas spreads out to fill all the space it has. Picking 'only to the bottom' mixes up a gas with a liquid.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: name one solid, one liquid and one gas in your kitchen.
items.a: For example: a steel plate (solid), coconut oil on a warm day (liquid) and the steam from the idli pot (gas).
items.why: A strong answer gives one of each and can say why: it keeps its shape, it flows, or it spreads out.

items.p: In the ice glove test, the glove was cut off. What shape was the ice?
items.why: The water froze in the shape of the glove. Ice is a solid, so it kept that shape after the glove was gone.
items.context: This question is about the ice glove test. You freeze water in a glove, peel the glove off, and watch the ice melt on a plate.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: the white cloud above a kettle is not real steam. What is it? Where is the real steam?
items.a: The white cloud is tiny drops of liquid water. The real steam is in the clear gap just above the spout, and it is invisible.
items.why: A strong answer says real steam is a gas you cannot see, and that it cools into tiny water drops a little higher up.
items.context: This question is about looking at a boiling kettle. A grown-up boils water, and you look for a clear gap just above the spout.

items.p: Fathima and Nandini are eating set curd from a katori.

views.says: Curd is a solid. I cut it with my spoon, and the cut keeps its shape.
Curd is a liquid. When Amma stirs it hard, it flows and takes the shape of the cup.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give one reason. Then say one thing the other girl has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason, and sees that both are partly right. Set curd holds a cut shape, but once it is stirred it flows.
items.why: Set curd is in between. Scientists call it a gel: a soft solid with a lot of liquid held inside. Stirring breaks it up, and then it flows like a thick liquid.

items.p: Put these in order, from coldest to hottest.
items.why: Ice is the coldest. As water warms up it melts, then gets warmer, then boils and turns into steam.

items.p: When ice gets warm and turns into water, we say it ____.
items.why: Melting is a solid changing into a liquid.

items.p: When water gets very cold and turns into ice, we say it ____.
items.why: Freezing is a liquid changing into a solid.

items.p: Draw the three bags turned upside down: the stone bag, the water bag and the air bag. Show where the stone, the water and the air are.
items.a: The stone at the new bottom of its bag, the water at the new bottom of its bag with a flat top, and the air bag still puffed full.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the solid and the liquid at the bottom, and the gas filling the whole bag.
items.context: This question is about the three bags. You fill one bag with a stone, one with water and one with air, then turn them upside down.
items.art: Three empty bag outlines, each drawn upside down.

items.p: When an ice cube melts, the water left behind weighs less than the ice did.
items.why: False. Melting changes the state, not the amount. The water weighs the same as the ice did.

items.p: Match each place to the state of the water there.
pairs: fog over the hills of Shillong
items.why: Water is in all three states around India. Fog, like the kettle cloud, is tiny drops of liquid water floating in the air.

items.p: Label the picture of a boiling kettle.
labels: the clear gap above the spout
a: clear gap: steam, a gas you cannot see
white cloud: tiny drops of liquid water
items.why: Real steam is invisible. It cools into tiny drops, and those drops make the white cloud.
items.context: This question is about looking at a boiling kettle. A grown-up boils water, and you look for a clear gap just above the spout.
items.art: A kettle on a stove with three label lines: one to the water inside, one to the clear gap above the spout, one to the white cloud.

items.p: Sumitra wants to make kulfi in the shape of a fish. What should she do?
opts: Pour the kulfi milk into a fish-shaped mould, then put the mould in the freezer
Freeze the milk in a bowl, then pour it into a fish mould
Pour frozen kulfi into a fish mould
items.why: Liquid milk takes the shape of the mould. When it freezes into a solid, it keeps that fish shape. Frozen kulfi is a solid, so it cannot be poured.

items.p: Kalpana's ice tray has 2 rows, with 6 little boxes in each row. How many ice cubes does she get?
items.why: 2 rows of 6 make 12. Each cube takes the shape of its little box, because the water was a liquid when she poured it in.

videos.title: Solids, liquids and gases for young children
videos.why: Shows solids keeping their shape, liquids pouring into new shapes and gases spreading out.
videos.check: Not yet found. Search for a short video on solids, liquids and gases for ages 6 to 8, and watch it first.

videos.title: The same water poured into different glasses: the conservation test
videos.why: Shows young children guessing that a tall glass holds more, like our pouring test.
videos.check: Not yet found. Search for a video of the Piaget liquid conservation task, and check that it shows the pouring back.

videos.title: Ice melting and water boiling, filmed up close
videos.why: Shows ice turning into water, and water boiling into steam, with the clear gap above the water.
videos.check: Not yet found. Search for a time-lapse of ice melting and a close-up of boiling water, and watch it first.

opts: It flows and takes the shape of its cup
It spreads out to fill the room
quiz.why: A solid, like a stone or an ice cube, keeps its own shape. Picking 'flows' mixes it up with a liquid.

quiz.p: Which of these is a liquid?
opts: Coconut oil on a hot day
quiz.why: On a hot day coconut oil flows and takes the shape of its bottle, so it is a liquid. A steel plate is a solid. Air is a gas.

quiz.p: Leela, a girl in Kochi, pours a tumbler of water into a wide plate with a rim. It looks very low. How much water is on the plate?
opts: Less than was in the tumbler
The same as was in the tumbler
More than was in the tumbler
quiz.why: Water takes the shape of the plate, so it spreads out low. The amount stays the same. Picking 'less' means judging the amount by the height.

quiz.p: Why did the water stand taller in the thin bottle?
opts: The bottle is narrow, so the same water has to stand higher
quiz.why: A narrow container has less room across, so the same amount of water stands taller.

quiz.p: In the three bags, which one filled the whole bag, even upside down?
quiz.why: Air is a gas, so it spreads out to fill all the space. The stone and the water went to the bottom.
Ice is frozen water. Let it melt and it becomes liquid water again. Nothing is added or taken away.
Real steam is water as a gas, and it is invisible. The white cloud is tiny drops of liquid water. Picking 'white' is what most people think.

quiz.p: Mohan, a boy in Pune, leaves an ice cube on a plate in a warm room. What happens to it?
opts: It melts into a flat pool of water
It stays a cube for ever
It turns into steam straight away
quiz.why: Warmth melts ice into water. The water has no shape of its own, so it spreads flat on the plate.

quiz.p: Why could the ice hand keep its shape after the glove was cut off?
opts: Ice is a solid, so it keeps its own shape
The glove was still inside it
The water was still a liquid
quiz.why: The water froze in the glove's shape. As a solid, it keeps that shape until it melts.

quiz.p: Before the pouring test, what should you do first?
opts: Guess what will happen, and say why
quiz.why: A guess with a reason helps you notice when the test surprises you.

applications: Moulds for kulfi, ice cubes and candles work because a liquid takes the shape of the mould, then sets into a solid that keeps that shape.
Pipes, taps and drains carry water, because a liquid flows.
Balloons, footballs and cycle tyres are filled with air, because a gas spreads out to fill them.
Idli pots and pressure cookers cook food with steam, which is water as a gas.
Cooking gas is squeezed into a cylinder as a liquid, so a lot fits in, and it comes out as a gas.

open_questions.q: How many states of matter are there?
open_questions.why_open: Solid, liquid and gas are the three we see most. Lightning and the Sun are made of plasma, a fourth state. Very cold states were predicted from the work of Satyendra Nath Bose of Kolkata, and first made in 1995. Scientists keep finding new ones, so nobody can say how many there are.

open_questions.q: What does liquid water look like on the inside?
open_questions.why_open: In ice, the water particles are lined up neatly. In liquid water, they keep joining and letting go very fast. Scientists still argue about exactly how they are arranged.

ask_kids: Is the sambar in the pot more than the sambar in your bowl? How would you check?
What solids are on your plate today? What liquids?

maths.problem: In the pouring test, Revathi filled her tumbler to the bindi with 8 spoons of water. She poured it into a thin bottle, then back. Then into a wide bowl, then back. How many spoons of water were in the tumbler at the end? What if 1 spoon stayed stuck to the walls each time?
maths.answer: 8 spoons if none were lost. If 1 spoon stayed behind each time, 6 spoons were left.
maths.explain: Pouring does not change the amount, so it stays 8. If 1 spoon is left on the walls twice, 8 take away 2 is 6. That is why we pour slowly and count the drips.
maths.context: This question is about the pouring test. You pour one tumbler of water into a tall, thin bottle and into a wide bowl, then pour it back to a bindi line on the tumbler.
maths.why_maths: Counting spoons shows the amount stayed the same, and taking away shows how much the drips can change the result.

maths.problem: Draw three columns: solid, liquid and gas. In the Home Hunt, Zoya found 5 solids, 4 liquids and 2 gases. Draw a block for each one. Which column is tallest? Which is shortest, and why do you think gases were the hardest to find?
maths.answer: Solids are tallest with 5 blocks. Gases are shortest with 2 blocks. Gases are hard to find because most of them are invisible.
maths.explain: 5 is more than 4, and 4 is more than 2. The short gas column tells us something about gases: we cannot see most of them, so we miss them.
maths.context: This question is about the Home Hunt. You walk around your home and find solids, liquids and gases.
maths.why_maths: Blocks in columns show at a glance which kind of thing was easiest to find, and make us ask why.

maths.problem: One ice tray has 2 rows of 7 little boxes. Ammu fills 2 trays. How many ice cubes does she get? If each cube is 2 spoons of water, how many spoons of water did she pour?
maths.answer: 28 ice cubes, and 56 spoons of water.
maths.explain: 2 rows of 7 make 14 cubes in one tray, and 2 trays make 28. Each cube is 2 spoons, so 28 cubes are 28 + 28 = 56 spoons. When they melt, they make 56 spoons of water again.
maths.context: This question is about making ice in an ice tray, where each little box holds water that freezes into a cube.
maths.why_maths: Equal groups tell us how many cubes, and how much water, without counting each one.

maths.problem: Megha has a tall, thin glass and a short, wide tumbler. She fills the thin glass with water and pours it into the wide tumbler. The wide tumbler is not full. Which holds more: the thin glass or the wide tumbler? How do you know?
maths.explain: All the water from the full thin glass fitted into the wide tumbler, with room left over. So the wide tumbler can hold more, even though it is shorter.
maths.context: This question is about the pouring test. You pour one tumbler of water into a tall, thin bottle and into a wide bowl, then pour it back to a bindi line on the tumbler.
maths.why_maths: Pouring from one container into another is a way to compare how much they hold, without being fooled by how tall they are.

warmup.q: Name a solid in this room.
warmup.a: A chair, a book, a steel tumbler, a door.

warmup.q: What does a liquid do when you pour it into a bowl?
warmup.a: It takes the shape of the bowl.

warmup.q: Is air a solid, a liquid or a gas?

warmup.a: No. It is invisible. The white cloud is tiny water drops.

warmup.q: Did the thin bottle make more water?
warmup.a: No. Poured back, it came to the same line.

roots.context: We have poured water into new shapes, squeezed bags of a stone, water and air, and looked for steam. Now we ask what that tells us about water, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: In your test, the water looked like more in the thin bottle and less in the wide bowl. Poured back, it reached the same bindi line each time. Water has no shape of its own, so it takes the shape of whatever holds it. How much water there is stays the same.
deep_truth.habit: We judge how much there is by how big or tall it looks. The pouring test showed that the height of the water came from the container, while the amount never changed.
deep_truth.evidence: In the pouring test, the water stood tall in the thin bottle and low in the wide bowl. Each time, poured back into the tumbler, it came to the bindi line.

three.who_am_i: More than half of your body is water. It is held inside your skin and inside the tiny cells that make you.
three.what_is_life: A plant stands up firm when the tiny cells in its stems and leaves are full of water. Without water, the plant droops.
three.what_is_this_world: The same water is ice on the Himalayas, liquid in the Kaveri river, and an invisible gas in the air of a monsoon day in Chennai.

roots.thread: Ice, liquid water and steam look completely different. Yet they are the same water, and nothing is added or taken away when one turns into another. Water particles only hold on to each other more tightly or more loosely. Everything is conscious, down to these tiny water particles.

teachings.teaching: Uddalaka tells his son Shvetaketu: when you know one lump of clay, you know everything made of clay. The things made from it have different names and shapes. What they really are is clay.
teachings.link: In our test, the water in the thin bottle and in the wide bowl had different shapes. What it really was, and how much of it there was, stayed the same.

teachings.teaching: The highest good is like water. Water helps all things and does not fight them. It flows to the low places.
teachings.link: In the three bags, the water always ran to the lowest part of its bag and fitted that shape. The Tao Te Ching, from China, praises water for fitting itself to whatever is around it.

science.text: On Earth, water is found naturally as a solid, a liquid and a gas: as ice and snow, as rivers and seas, and as invisible water vapour in the air.
Scientists still argue about exactly how the particles of liquid water are arranged, because they join and let go of each other very fast.

other_view.view: They say a drop of water has no awareness at all. They explain everything water does with particles and forces, and they find no need for a mind to explain it.

practice.title: Water in your hands
practice.say: Stand at the sink or over a bucket. Cup your two hands together, and I will pour in a little water. Feel the water fill your hands. It takes the shape of your hands. Now open your fingers a little. Feel the water slip out between them. Take three slow breaths while it drains away. Notice how your hands feel now.
practice.kid: Cup your hands over the sink. Let a grown-up pour in a little water. Feel it fill your hands. Open your fingers a little. Feel it slip away. Breathe slowly three times.

ask: When the water was in your hands, was its shape the water's or your hands'?
Ice, water and steam look so different. What makes them the same water?
Your body is more than half water. Does that water take your shape, or do you take its shape?

science: Solids, liquids and gases: standard primary science (for example Cambridge Primary Science and NCERT Environmental Studies).
Conservation of liquid quantity: J. Piaget and A. Szeminska, La genese du nombre chez l'enfant (1941). Young children often judge the amount of liquid by its height.
Water vapour is invisible. The visible plume above boiling water is condensed droplets, which form a short distance above the spout.
Ice is about 9 percent larger in volume than the liquid water it froze from, so it floats.
Galileo Galilei, Discourse on Bodies that Stay Atop Water, or Move in It (1612), written after the 1611 dispute in Florence about why ice floats.
LPG is stored in cylinders as a liquid under pressure and leaves the valve as a gas.
More than half of the human body by mass is water (roughly 50 to 60 percent in adults, more in children).
Bose-Einstein condensates were predicted from the work of S. N. Bose and A. Einstein (1924 to 1925) and first made in 1995.
Ice stupas in Ladakh: artificial cone-shaped glaciers built in winter to store water for spring irrigation (from about 2014).
The structure of liquid water is still an active research question.

playtest: Thought through as a parent and child in a flat. The pouring test: a glass tumbler filled halfway (about 100 to 120 ml) fits in a 200 or 250 ml drink bottle through a funnel, where it stands clearly taller, and in a wide bowl it lies about a finger deep. Poured back over a tray, it returns to the bindi or a hair below it, from drops on the walls. Most tray ice cubes are too big for a drink bottle mouth, and a note covers a smaller cube. The three bags work with any clear food bag. The kettle gap of one or two finger-widths is easy to see against something dark, with the child one big step back. The ice glove freezes overnight in most freezers, and its fingers melt on a plate in a warm room in under an hour. The spine is the intro, the three bags and the pouring test (session 1, about 37 minutes), then the explanations, Roots and the quiz (session 2, about 30 minutes). This is the first unit on this subtopic, so it leads on from the Class 2 properties of materials unit. It avoids the Class 3 states units: no dissolving, no syrup race or drops on a coin, no closed box or drops on a lid, no salt crystals, and no orange peel smell race, which the atoms unit uses.
